headline: Jeffrey's in 150 feet: cod holding the gravel edge, haddock buried in the mud at Platts
subhead: A steady week of structure fishing on the Ledge — nothing explosive, but the depths are sorting fish exactly where they should be in late July.
body_markdown:
One-fifty feet, hard gravel, the edge where Jeffrey's Ledge falls off toward the basin — that's been my starting mark all week, and it's still the most consistent water I've got. Cod don't sit on flat gravel, they sit on the transition, right where the rock breaks up and rolls into softer bottom. Mark that seam on the sounder, drop a diamond jig or a high-low rig baited with clam, and you're in business. Fish have been running 24 to 30 inches, a few pushing better than that, with the biggest one I weighed this week going 14 pounds off a boat out of Rye running the same stretch I fish north of the Ledge tower.

Haddock's a different story and a different bottom entirely. I've been working Platts Bank in 220 to 250 feet of soft mud, and that's where the haddock want to be this time of year — head down in the current, feeding on whatever's drifting through on the tide. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid or clam belly have been the ticket, worked with a short lift-drop right off bottom. Don't work it too hard. Haddock feed close to the mud, and if you're ripping the jig two and three feet off bottom you're fishing over their heads. Fish have been coming up in that 20 to 24 inch class, clean and fat, with decent numbers — not a slam dunk trip, but if you find the right drift and hold the boat on it, you can put a good box together.

Pollock have scattered up in the water column over structure between Jeffrey's and Tillies Bank, 80 to 110 feet down over bottom that reads 130 to 160. These fish are chasing bait higher than they were a month ago — I've marked them suspended, not glued to bottom, which tells me the mackerel and herring pushed them up. Jigging a bucktail or a Norwegian-style jig through that mid-water column has been the move, and it's been a nice change of pace from bottom fishing — pollock hit hard and don't quit pulling. Hake are still down in the mud holes of Scantum Basin, best worked at first light or the last hour of daylight, and that's been more of a night-bite pattern lately as the water's stayed warm on top.

Mackerel have been thick on the surface out on the Ledge — not a fishery in themselves for most of my guys, but they matter. Where the mackerel are balled up, that's where everything else is staged underneath, and it's also bait for the tuna gear if you're carrying a spread. Whales have been working the same bait pockets between Jeffrey's and the Stellwagen approaches, which is as good a sign as any that the forage base out there is healthy right now.

On the bluefin — it's early yet. The real giant fishery on the Ledge doesn't usually turn on until October, when the bait balls up tight and the big fish push in behind it. What we've had this week is scattered sign: a few boats marking singles rolling on bait between Jeffrey's and the Stellwagen line, likely early scouts riding a warm filament that's pushed up from the south. I wouldn't build a trip around it yet. If you're out there groundfishing and you see fish up, it's worth a look, but the real window is still two months out.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady, if unspectacular, structure fishing through the stretch, and that's exactly what's played out. Nobody's filling the box in twenty minutes, but if you know your bottom and fish the right depth for the right species, you're coming home with fish. That's the Ledge in late July — it rewards patience and precision, not luck.

Tide's been building as the moon works toward full in early August, and that's actually helped. Stronger current means the haddock on Platts hold tighter to structure and the cod on the gravel edge feed more aggressively during the peak of the push. I'd plan around the bigger tide swings this coming week rather than fighting slack water — get out to the Ledge or Platts on the front half of the flood or the back half of the ebb, when the current's really moving, and you'll see better marks and better hookup ratios.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change in the next few days. Cod will keep holding the gravel edges around Jeffrey's, haddock will stay buried in the mud out at Platts and up into the Basin, and pollock will keep suspending over structure wherever the bait sits. If the wind stays out of the southwest like it has been, it'll keep laying flat enough to run out comfortable from Rye, and that's really all you need this time of year — clean water, the right depth, and the patience to fish it properly. I'd keep an eye on the mackerel schools too. When they thin out or move, that usually tells you the bigger fish underneath are about to shift with them.
